blocks.html: INTRODUCTION
1. —
The aim of the present seminar is twofold.

On the one hand, we aim to provide convenient foundations for the theory of group schemes in general. Exposés I to IV will supply in this regard the indispensable preliminary exercises in schematic and categorical syntax. In order to obtain a language that "sticks" effortlessly to geometric intuition, and to avoid circumlocutions that become unbearable in the long run, we shall always identify a prescheme \(X\) over another \(S\) with the functor \((\mathrm{Sch})^\circ_{/S} \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) that it represents∗, and it is necessary to frame many definitions in such a way that they apply to arbitrary functors, representable or not. Moreover, almost all the functors we shall have occasion to use will be "sheaves" (for the "faithfully flat quasi-compact topology"); Exposé IV, which deals with groups only incidentally, gives an outline of the language of "localization" and of sheaves, which proves equally convenient in questions of representability of functors. Above all, this exposé will provide us, for questions of passage to the quotient, with the most convenient framework for the sequel. Exposé V gives some general results on the existence of quotients, taken up again in Exposé VIA in the case of the quotient of an algebraic group over a field (or more generally, over an artinian ring) by a subgroup∗∗. This last exposé and Exposé VIB which follows it also contain various elementary results special to algebraic groups over a field, currently used in the sequel. Exposé VII studies certain facts connected with the characteristic of the base field and develops in particular, with the appropriate generality, the correspondence between radicial group schemes of height 1 and restricted \(p\)-Lie algebras. Finally, Exposé
XVIII contains the generalization, in the theory of schemes, of Weil's theorem on the "birational" definition of algebraic groups.

On the other hand, we propose to generalize to groups over an arbitrary base prescheme the Borel-Chevalley structure theory of affine algebraic groups. It became apparent, moreover, in the course of writing up the notes of the seminar, that the affineness hypothesis was superfluous for many results of the theory. The most complete results are obtained, of course, in the case of "semi-simple group schemes", or more generally "reductive" ones, with which we shall be exclusively concerned from Exposé XIX onwards. Chevalley himself had already given the construction of the "Tôhoku" groups over the ring of integers, a construction which will be taken up again in the present seminar. The principal uniqueness theorem gives a simple characterization of the "twisted" variants of these Tôhoku groups over a base prescheme \(S\): they are the groups affine and smooth over \(S\) whose geometric fibres are connected semi-simple groups in the usual sense∗∗∗.

footnotes.html: (∗) Such a point of view seems to have been envisaged for the first time eight or nine years ago in connection with the theory of formal groups by P. Cartier, who unfortunately did not take the trouble to make it precise and to systematize it as it deserved.

(∗∗) For a more thorough study of passage to the quotient, notably by reductive groups, see the important study of D. MUMFORD, Geometric Invariant Theory, Ergebnisse der Mathematik, Bd 34, Springer 1965. Let us observe that on one important point the terminology of that book does not agree with ours, for over a field of characteristic \(p > 0\), the groups that Mumford calls "reductive" are the smooth groups of multiplicative type in the sense of the Seminar. One may doubtless hold that Mumford's acceptation of the word "reductive", which loses its meaning over a base that is not a field, was adopted by him provisionally and as a kind of makeshift (and this is also roughly what Mumford explains, on other grounds, from the second paragraph of his preface onwards!).
(∗∗∗) This is the essential result of the thesis of M. Demazure (schémas en groupes réductifs, Bull. de la Soc. Math. de France, 1965, p. 369–413).

blocks.html: 2. —

As in the case of the theory known over an algebraically closed field, a crucial role is played by the subtori of the group schemes under consideration. Accordingly the preliminary study of tori, and more generally of "group schemes of multiplicative type" (both from the intrinsic point of view and from the point of view of the subgroups of multiplicative type of a given group), takes up a fairly large place in this Seminar (Exposés VIII to XII). Their remarkable rigidity (even greater in certain respects than that of abelian schemes, or of semi-simple schemes) makes them very efficient working tools for the study of certain more general groups.
3. —

From Exposé XII onwards (with the exception of Exposé XVIII already mentioned) we shall make current use of the theory of affine algebraic groups over an algebraically closed field, which the reader will find in the Séminaire CHEVALLEY 1956, more particularly in Exposés IV to IX of that Seminar. We shall also use, though to a lesser extent, the later exposés of the Séminaire CHEVALLEY, devoted to the structure of semi-simple algebraic groups. Indeed, we shall take up CHEVALLEY's theory directly within the framework of schemes: it will be seen that in this way (even over a base field) the exposition gains in simplicity and in precision.
4. —

The principal object of the present Seminar is of course to develop techniques applicable to the study of group schemes over an arbitrary base, i.e. essentially to the study of families of algebraic groups. In this connection, the infinitesimal properties of such families, and in particular the case of an artinian base scheme, play an important role. These properties come into play even for the study of algebraic groups over a field \(k\), in the case where the latter is not perfect, notably in order to be able to apply the technique of descent in the non-Galois case.

Among the new results obtained in this case, let us mention the existence of maximal tori and of Cartan subgroups in an arbitrary smooth algebraic group, the rationality of the variety of maximal tori, and various related results (Exp. XIV), or the correspondence between the "forms" of a semi-simple group and the principal homogeneous bundles under a suitable (in general non-connected) semi-simple algebraic group (Exp. XXIV). In a general way, one may say that the methods required in order to work over a non-perfect base field are essentially those used for arbitrary base preschemes, and thereby fall outside the framework of classical algebraic geometry.
5. —

It has not seemed useful to indicate at the head of the written exposés the date or dates of the corresponding oral exposés of the Seminar. Let us be content to say that the order of the mimeographed exposés (from I to XXVI) does indeed correspond to the order of the oral exposés. Furthermore, the writing up of the definitive text is sometimes markedly later than that of the oral exposé, and often differs from it quite substantially, the written text being generally more detailed and more complete (such as Exp. IV and VIIB), or even appreciably more general (such as Exp. XII or VIIB) than the oral exposé. Other written exposés correspond to no oral exposé at all (VIB, VIIA, XV, XVI, XVII, and the essential part of XXVI), and were written and inserted into the mimeographed Seminar either to furnish convenient references for various other exposés (this is notably the case of VIB), or because they constitute a natural prolongation of the notions and techniques already developed. It will be noted as a consequence that the reading of Exposés VIIA, VIIB, XV, XVI, XVII is not necessary for the study of the rest of the Seminar, and in particular for the part of this Seminar devoted to reductive group schemes.
6. —

Of the theory of schemes, we shall use above all the general language of schemes, expounded in EGA I, the notions of flat morphism, étale morphism, smooth morphism, expounded in SGA 1, I to V, and finally the theory of faithfully flat descent of SGA 1, VIII. We have as far as possible avoided formulating superfluous noetherian hypotheses, which has obliged us in return to replace the usual hypothesis "of finite type" by the hypothesis "of finite presentation". For the notion of morphism of finite presentation, the reader should consult EGA IV 1∗∗∗∗. The results of SGA 1, I to IV, stated most often in the noetherian context, will be developed in the general case in EGA IV∗∗∗∗, where there will also be developed in detail standard methods for reducing certain types of statements (involving hypotheses of finite presentation) to the noetherian case (EGA, paragraphs 8, 9, 11). The reader who does not wish to grant these results of EGA IV will be able to simplify certain statements or their proof by assuming the base prescheme locally noetherian. He exposes himself, however, to difficulties in the cases where the proof proceeds by descent from \(\widehat{A}\) to \(A\), where \(\widehat{A}\) is the completion of a noetherian local ring \(A\), for this method leads one to introduce the (in general non-noetherian) ring \(\widehat{A} \otimes_A \widehat{A}\).

footnotes.html: (∗∗∗∗) Since the writing of this introduction, the four parts (§§ 1 to 21) of EGA IV have appeared.

blocks.html: 7. —

References will be made according to the usual decimal system: the reference 5.7.11 refers to the proposition (or lemma, definition…) of that name in the same exposé; in the reference XVII 7.8 the roman numeral indicates the number of the exposé. We shall use the following abbreviations for our standard references:

BIBLE = Séminaire CHEVALLEY "Groupes de Lie algébriques", 1956/58
EGA X.Y.Z = J. DIEUDONNÉ and A. GROTHENDIECK, Éléments de Géométrie Algébrique, Chap. X, par. Y, No. Z.
SGA X Y = Séminaire de Géométrie Algébrique du Bois-Marie, year X, exposé Y.
TDTE = A. GROTHENDIECK, Techniques de descente et Théorèmes d'existence en Géométrie Algébrique, exposés in the Séminaire Bourbaki between 1959 and 1962.
